title: Sharding
explain: Sharding splits one dataset across several nodes so that each node owns a disjoint subset of the keys and serves only that subset. It is how I scale writes and storage, which replicas cannot, because replicas copy everything. The real decisions are the shard key and how it maps to a shard.
model:
```
key --(shard key mapping)--> shard 1 | shard 2 | shard 3     (disjoint key sets)
```

Ways to choose the shard:

| Method | Good for | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hash** (`hash(key) % N`, ring, slot table) | even spread | no range scans; resharding moves keys |
| **Key range** (1-100, 101-200) | range scans | sequential keys pile onto one shard |
| **Time range** | cheap expiry of old data | today's shard takes all writes |
| **Tenant** / **geo** / **business key** | queries stay on one shard | uneven sizes, big tenants |

Three points follow every design:
1. **Skew is inevitable:** change the key, [salt](#/sd/f/salting) hot keys, or auto-split a big or busy shard into sub-shards.
2. **Scaling out moves data:** see [token rebalancing](#/sd/f/token-rebalancing), [consistent hashing](#/sd/f/consistent-hashing).
3. **Cross-shard transactions are expensive:** pick a key that keeps data written together on one shard before reaching for 2PC.

Logical units versus physical placement: [partitioning](#/sd/f/partitioning).

details.q: Why shard instead of adding replicas?
details.a: Replicas copy the whole dataset, so they scale reads and availability but not writes or storage. Sharding gives each node only a slice, so write throughput and capacity grow with node count.

details.q: An events table is sharded by created_at month and mostly written with new data. What is wrong?
details.a: Every write targets the newest shard, so one shard is a hotspot while older ones idle. Time-range sharding makes retention cheap (drop an old shard) and range scans easy, but monotonically increasing keys concentrate current writes.

details.q: The cluster uses hash(key) % N and grows from 4 to 5 shards. How many keys keep their shard?
details.a: About 20%: a key stays only if h mod 4 equals h mod 5, which holds for 4 of every 20 hash values. So 80% move, which is why modulo hashing suits a fixed shard count; use a ring or fixed bucket table instead.

details.q: One celebrity account makes one shard take 60% of traffic. What helps?
details.a: Salt the hot key so its load spreads over several shards and merge on read, auto-split the shard by size or load, or choose a key that spreads that entity. Adding replicas helps reads only; every write still lands on the same primary.

details.q: Order and placing an order must decrement stock atomically, but orders shard by order_id and inventory by sku. First move?
details.a: Choose shard keys that co-locate data written together, and use cross-shard coordination only for what remains. Cross-shard transactions are slow and fragile; 2PC is the fallback, not the opener.

details.q: How do you split an overloaded shard without downtime?
details.a: Detect the threshold, create the sub-shard and copy the upper key range while the old shard still serves, catch up on writes during the copy, switch routing for that range, then delete the moved range from the old shard. Delete last so you keep a fallback.

details.q: How do you pick a shard key?
details.a: Ask which queries and transactions are most common and keep them on one shard, then check cardinality and skew. A good key spreads load evenly, matches the access pattern, and is hard to change later.

prompts.q: Explain sharding and how it differs from replication.
points: Each node owns a disjoint subset of keys
Replicas copy everything and scale reads and availability
The shard key and mapping are the key decisions

prompts.q: Compare the common ways to choose a shard and the failure mode of each.
points: Hash: even, no range scans, resharding
Time range: newest shard is hot but expiry is cheap
Tenant, geo, business key: locality but uneven sizes

prompts.q: Your sharded system has a hot shard and needs to grow. Describe how you handle skew, rebalancing and cross-shard transactions.
points: Skew: change key, salt hot keys, auto-split
Rebalancing: move data while the old owner still serves, then switch
Co-locate data written together to avoid 2PC
Saga or 2PC only for what cannot be co-located
